questions.q: Why do base Lightning components give developers an accessibility baseline with no extra work?
options: Because accessibility is not actually required in Salesforce orgs
Because base components disable all ARIA attributes by default
Because they're built on SLDS markup following the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, and they update their own ARIA attributes automatically as state changes
Because base components cannot be customized at all, which coincidentally avoids accessibility bugs
questions.explain: Base components already follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide and automatically manage their own ARIA state (like aria-invalid), which is accessibility work the developer doesn't have to redo correctly from scratch.

questions.q: Per Salesforce's documented guidance, when should `aria-label` be used instead of visible text?
options: Only when a visible label genuinely isn't possible, such as an icon-only button -- visible text is preferred whenever it's an option
aria-label should always be preferred over visible text, for every control
aria-label and visible text must always be used together on every element
aria-label is never appropriate in LWC templates
questions.explain: The documented priority is visible text first; aria-label is the fallback specifically for cases like icon-only controls where visible text isn't an option, since aria-label itself isn't visible to sighted users.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `slds-assistive-text` and `display: none` for hiding content?
options: There is no difference; both hide content identically from everyone
slds-assistive-text can only be used inside base components, never in custom markup
display: none is the SLDS-recommended approach, and slds-assistive-text is deprecated
slds-assistive-text visually hides content while keeping it announced by screen readers; display: none removes it from assistive technology entirely
questions.explain: slds-assistive-text hides content visually but keeps it available to screen readers -- exactly the opposite of display: none (or aria-hidden), which removes the content from assistive technology as well.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend regarding tab order and the `tabindex` attribute?
options: Use tabindex liberally to create a fully custom tab order for every component
tabindex should be set to a high positive number on every focusable element
Let the natural DOM order in the template drive tab order; avoid using tabindex to force a different sequence
Tab order has no relationship to DOM order in LWC templates
questions.explain: DOM order should drive tab order naturally. Forcing a different order with tabindex tends to create a confusing, hard-to-maintain sequence for keyboard and assistive-technology users.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the visible focus indicator should never be removed with CSS?
options: Because the focus ring is how a keyboard-only user tracks their current position on the page -- removing it makes the component unusable for keyboard navigation
Because removing it is technically impossible in any browser
Because the focus indicator is required for SLDS styling to apply at all
Because it only affects screen readers, not keyboard users
questions.explain: A visible focus indicator is the primary way a keyboard-only user can tell which element currently has focus. Removing it with CSS breaks keyboard navigation usability entirely for that component.
